zh.q: 显微镜下，小炭粒为什么会自己动起来？
zh.concl: 悬浮在液体中的微粒做无规则的、不停息的运动，这就是布朗运动；1827 年布朗首先在显微镜下研究它。微粒太小、肉眼看不到，必须用高倍显微镜，结果还可以通过显示器呈现（教材 p.3–4）。
points: 看到的是悬浮的微粒（约 10⁻⁶ m 级），不是分子——分子约 0.1 nm 级，光学显微镜根本分辨不了；微粒的运动只是分子撞击的间接证据（教材 p.4 旁注）。
必须用高倍显微镜：教材演示调至 400 倍或 1 000 倍，目镜里的结果可以通过显示器呈现（p.3）。
没有定向漂移：它东一步、西一步，方向随时在变，不是被水流冲着走。

zh.q: 把它的位置每 30 秒记一次，连起来是什么样子？
zh.concl: 每隔 30 s 记下一个位置，再用线段按时间顺序连起来，就得到教材图 1.1-4 那样的折线。折线不等于真实路径——教材 p.4 说得明白：「就是在 30 s 内，微粒的运动也是极不规则的」。
points: 记录间隔 30 s 是教材给的值（p.4），不是「微粒每 30 s 才动一下」。
折线只是采样连线：两个记录点之间，微粒照样在乱走（放大视窗里能看到那段锯齿）。
净位移 16.50 μm 远小于路程 64.8 μm——它东一步西一步，大部分互相抵消了。

zh.q: 记录时间从 2 分钟延到 10 分钟，均方位移怎么变？
zh.concl: 均方位移与时间成正比（⟨r²⟩ = 4Dt，二维投影；属拓展 L3，教材本节没有公式），所以均方根位移只按 √t 增长，而折线的路程按 t 增长——三个量不能混。
points: ⟨r²⟩ ∝ t：时间 5 倍，均方位移就 5 倍。
均方根位移 √⟨r²⟩ ∝ √t，只长到约 √5 倍。
折线总路程 L ∝ t，跟时间同倍长——路程长不等于「走得远」。

zh.q: 换一颗更小的炭粒，运动是更明显还是更不明显？
zh.concl: 教材 p.4：微粒越小，某一瞬间跟它相撞的液体分子数越少，撞击作用的不平衡性就表现得越明显；并且微粒越小，它的质量越小，运动状态越容易被改变——所以布朗运动越明显。教材的反例：微粒很大时各方向撞击接近平衡，就很难观察到布朗运动了。
points: 撞击数 N ∝ r²（示意）：3.86 × 10¹⁵ → 6.17 × 10¹⁴，微粒越小，一个时间窗里被撞的次数越少。
质量 ∝ r³：同样的净力，微粒越小加速度越大，运动状态越容易被改变。

zh.q: 把悬浊液从 20 ℃ 加热到 100 ℃，运动变化有多大？
zh.concl: 教材 p.3 的演示「改变悬浊液的温度。重复上述操作」给出结论：温度越高，小炭粒的运动越明显；p.4「温度是分子热运动剧烈程度的标志」。定量上（拓展）液体粘度随温度下降、粘滞阻力变小，D ∝ T/η(T) 涨 4.5807 倍，比只看 T 的 1.2730 倍强得多。示意：本课把温度取到 100 ℃ 只是把趋势画到底——真实悬浊液到 100 ℃ 会沸腾、出现对流，显微镜下反而看不到稳定的布朗运动。
points: 温度越高，分子无规则运动越剧烈，撞微粒撞得更凶。
液体粘度随温度下降（1.005 → 0.279 mPa·s，掉到 1/3.5982），粘滞阻力变小、同样的撞击涨落推得更远。
两条合起来，均方位移涨 4.5807 倍——比只看 T 的 1.2730 倍强得多。

zh.q: 微粒为什么一会儿往这边、一会儿往那边？
zh.concl: 教材 p.4（图 1.1-5）：液体分子不停地做无规则运动，不断地撞击微粒；某一瞬间微粒在某个方向受到的撞击作用较强，在下一瞬间又受到另一方向的撞击作用较强，这样就引起了微粒无规则的运动。悬浮微粒的无规则运动并不是分子的运动，但可以间接反映液体分子运动的无规则性。
points: 撞击极密（示意：每毫秒约 3.86 × 10¹⁵ 次），不平衡极其微小（相对涨落 1.61 × 10⁻⁸），但合力总不为零。
合力方向一直在变：这一瞬间偏左、下一瞬间偏右，所以微粒东一步西一步。
窗里能看到：30 s 内它走过的路是密密麻麻的锯齿——折线上那两个记录点之间的「直线」只是没被记录下来。

zh.q: 换一颗微粒再测一遍，均方位移会变吗？
zh.concl: 布朗运动是统计规律：单次结果涨落很大，只有大量微粒（或很多次）平均起来，⟨r²⟩ 才稳定。教材图 1.1-4 画三颗微粒、三条形状完全不同的折线，正是这件事。
points: 同一颗微粒、同一工况，每次读数逐位相同（带种子的随机数，不是每次重掷骰子）。
换一颗微粒：净位移 16.50 → 29.26 μm，差了近一倍——这是单次结果的涨落。
⟨r²⟩ = 4Dt 是统计平均，不随单次结果变：512.3 μm² 一直在那儿。

zh.q: 一杯静水里滴一滴墨，为什么过一会儿周围都变黑了？
zh.concl: 教材 p.3：扩散现象并不是外界作用（例如对流、重力作用等）引起的，也不是化学反应的结果，而是由物质分子的无规则运动产生的，是分子永不停息地做无规则运动的证据之一；p.4「温度越高，扩散得越快」——同样观察时刻，100 ℃ 的扩散宽度是 20 ℃ 的近两倍，而峰高只剩一半：面积守恒，峰矮了就变宽。
points: 扩散靠分子热运动，不需要搅拌，也不是化学反应。
峰变矮、曲线变宽是同一件事：浓度曲线的面积守恒。
温度升高扩散更快：墨水的扩散系数 500.00 → 2290.34 μm²·s⁻¹（20 ℃ → 100 ℃）。

zh.q: 想让这颗炭粒的均方位移达到 2000 μm² 以上，怎么调？
zh.concl: 温度升高或换更小的微粒，都能让 ⟨r²⟩ 变大：20 ℃、0.5 μm 是 512.3 μm²，100 ℃ 同一颗是 2346.6 μm²；半径从 0.5 减到 0.2 μm 得 1280.7 μm²。教材的结论「温度越高、微粒越小，运动越明显」在这里变成一个能达成的目标。
points: 两条路都行：升温，或换更小的微粒——都让 ⟨r²⟩ = 4Dt 变大。
判据是统计量 ⟨r²⟩ 的期望值，不是屏上这一条随机轨迹的 r²（单条轨迹涨落很大）。
只加记录次数不够：次数上限 20 次（10 分钟）也只有 1024.6 μm²。

en.q: Under the microscope, why does a small carbon particle move on its own?
en.concl: Particles suspended in a liquid move randomly and ceaselessly; this is Brownian motion, first studied under a microscope by Brown in 1827. The particles are too small for the naked eye, so a high-power microscope is needed, and the results can be shown on a monitor (textbook pp.3–4).
points: What you see are suspended particles (on the order of 10⁻⁶ m), not molecules; molecules are on the order of 0.1 nm, far beyond what an optical microscope can resolve; the particles' motion is only indirect evidence of molecular impacts (textbook p.4 margin note).
A high-power microscope is needed: the textbook demonstration uses 400× or 1 000×, and what's seen in the eyepiece can be shown on a monitor (p.3).
There's no steady drift: it steps one way, then another, changing direction constantly, not carried along by a current.

en.q: Record its position every 30 seconds and join the points: what does it look like?
en.concl: Record a position every 30 s and join them in time order with line segments to get a zigzag like textbook Fig. 1.1-4. The zigzag isn't the real path; textbook p.4 says it clearly: "even within 30 s, the particle's motion is extremely irregular".
points: The 30 s recording interval is the textbook's value (p.4), not "the particle only moves every 30 s".
The zigzag only joins samples: between two recorded points the particle keeps wandering (the jagged path is visible in the magnified window).
The net displacement of 16.50 μm is far less than the path length of 64.8 μm; it steps one way then another, and most steps cancel out.

en.q: Extend the recording from 2 to 10 minutes: how does the mean squared displacement change?
en.concl: Mean squared displacement is proportional to time (⟨r²⟩ = 4Dt, 2D projection; extension L3, no formula in this textbook section), so the root mean square displacement grows only as √t, while the zigzag length grows as t; the three quantities must not be mixed up.
points: ⟨r²⟩ ∝ t: 5 times the time gives 5 times the mean squared displacement.
Root mean square displacement √⟨r²⟩ ∝ √t, only about √5 times larger.
Total zigzag length L ∝ t grows in step with time; a long path doesn't mean "going far".

en.q: With a smaller carbon particle, is the motion more or less pronounced?
en.concl: Textbook p.4: the smaller the particle, the fewer liquid molecules hit it at any instant and the more pronounced the imbalance of impacts; also, the smaller the particle, the smaller its mass and the more easily its motion changes, so Brownian motion is more pronounced. The textbook's counterexample: when the particle is very large, impacts from all directions nearly balance and Brownian motion is hard to observe.
points: Number of impacts N ∝ r² (schematic): 3.86 × 10¹⁵ → 6.17 × 10¹⁴; the smaller the particle, the fewer hits in a time window.
Relative fluctuation δ = 1/√N ∝ 1/r: smaller means more unbalanced (1.61 × 10⁻⁸ → 4.03 × 10⁻⁸, exactly 2.5 times = 0.5 / 0.2).
Mass ∝ r³: for the same net force, a smaller particle accelerates more and its motion changes more easily.

en.q: Heat the suspension from 20 ℃ to 100 ℃: how much does the motion change?
en.concl: The textbook p.3 demonstration "change the temperature of the suspension and repeat" concludes: the higher the temperature, the more pronounced the carbon particles' motion; p.4 "temperature is a measure of how vigorous molecular thermal motion is". Quantitatively (extension), liquid viscosity falls with temperature and viscous drag decreases, so D ∝ T/η(T) grows 4.5807 times, far more than the 1.2730 times from T alone. Illustrative: this lesson takes the temperature to 100 ℃ only to draw the trend to the end; a real suspension would boil and convect at 100 ℃, and no steady Brownian motion would be seen under the microscope.
points: The higher the temperature, the more vigorous the random motion of molecules and the harder they hit the particle.
Liquid viscosity falls with temperature (1.005 → 0.279 mPa·s, down to 1/3.5982), viscous drag drops, and the same impact fluctuations push the particle farther.
Together the two raise the mean squared displacement 4.5807 times, far more than the 1.2730 times from T alone.

en.q: Why does the particle go this way one moment and that way the next?
en.concl: Textbook p.4 (Fig. 1.1-5): liquid molecules move randomly and ceaselessly and keep hitting the particle; at one instant the impacts are stronger from one direction, at the next from another, and this causes the particle's random motion. The random motion of suspended particles isn't the motion of molecules, but it indirectly reflects the randomness of liquid molecular motion.
points: Impacts are extremely frequent (schematic: about 3.86 × 10¹⁵ per millisecond) and the imbalance extremely small (relative fluctuation 1.61 × 10⁻⁸), but the net force is never zero.
The direction of the net force keeps changing: left one instant, right the next, so the particle steps one way then another.
In the window you can see that its path over 30 s is a dense jagged line; the "straight line" between two recorded points on the zigzag is just what wasn't recorded.

en.q: Measure a different particle: does the mean squared displacement change?
en.concl: Brownian motion follows a statistical law: single results fluctuate widely, and only averaging over many particles (or many runs) makes ⟨r²⟩ stable. Textbook Fig. 1.1-4 draws three particles with three completely different zigzags for exactly this reason.
points: Same particle, same conditions: every reading matches digit for digit (seeded random numbers, not a fresh roll of the dice each time).
Change the particle: net displacement 16.50 → 29.26 μm, nearly double; that's the fluctuation of a single result.
⟨r²⟩ = 4Dt is a statistical average and doesn't change with single results: 512.3 μm² stays put.

en.q: Drop some ink into a glass of still water: why does everything around it turn dark after a while?
en.concl: Textbook p.3: diffusion is not caused by external action (such as convection or gravity) and is not a chemical reaction; it arises from the random motion of molecules and is one piece of evidence that molecules move randomly and ceaselessly; p.4 "the higher the temperature, the faster the diffusion"; at the same moment, the diffusion width at 100 ℃ is nearly twice that at 20 ℃, and the peak is only half as high: the area is conserved, so a lower peak means a wider spread.
points: Diffusion relies on molecular thermal motion; it needs no stirring and isn't a chemical reaction.
A lower peak and a wider curve are the same thing: the area under the concentration curve is conserved.
Higher temperature, faster diffusion: the ink's diffusion coefficient 500.00 → 2290.34 μm²·s⁻¹ (20 ℃ → 100 ℃).

en.q: How would you get this carbon particle's mean squared displacement above 2000 μm²?
en.concl: Raising the temperature or using a smaller particle both increase ⟨r²⟩: 512.3 μm² at 20 ℃ and 0.5 μm, 2346.6 μm² for the same particle at 100 ℃; reducing the radius from 0.5 to 0.2 μm gives 1280.7 μm². The textbook's conclusion "the higher the temperature and the smaller the particle, the more pronounced the motion" becomes an achievable goal here.
points: Either path works: raise the temperature, or use a smaller particle; both make ⟨r²⟩ = 4Dt larger.
The criterion is the expected value of the statistic ⟨r²⟩, not the r² of the single random trajectory on screen (a single trajectory fluctuates a lot).
Just adding records isn't enough: even the maximum of 20 records (10 minutes) gives only 1024.6 μm².
